subject: US Economics Analyst: What Is the Best Way to Measure Inflation?
summary: The conceptual starting point is that the best measure depends on the purpose. **A cost-of-living index like CPI, a GDP deflator like PCE, and a central bank's ideal gauge are three different objects, and PCE was built for the second job, not the third.** Because PCE must cover everything counted as consumption in the national accounts, it carries prices consumers never see — employer-paid healthcare, nonprofit spending, some financial-services fees — and even lets stock-market swings move measured inflation through asset-based fees. Quality adjustment adds another wedge: phones and TVs register as deflation after adjusting for quality even as consumers perceive rising sticker prices, and insurance price changes driven by a worse risk pool read as no change in the official data.

Its main value is historical contrast — more alarming than core in 2022, less so by mid-2023 — rather than a different reading today, where it nearly matches core.

subject: Global Markets Analyst: 10 Questions on Coordinated Yen Intervention
summary: The case. - **The intervention is a real but temporary reprieve; only fundamentals can make it durable.** It was a strong stabilizing step, but without a material change in the global growth outlook or Japan's domestic policy mix, the effect fades. When forecasts point to a structurally higher policy path, the survey model assigns more of any rise in long yields to expected rates and less to premium — hence the lower, steadier estimates. **The clearest payoff is Japan, where the survey model recognises that rising surveyed policy-rate projections, alongside inflation expectations converging on 2%, explain much of the JGB bear steepening that the yield curve-only model would book almost entirely as term premium.** Germany after the March 2025 debt brake reform is a similar case: surveys captured an upgraded growth outlook and a structurally higher path for real rates, so the survey model showed a smaller premium jump — though only once the March survey landed, illustrating the lag cost of lower-frequency inputs.

summary: Backdrop. The FOMC signals policy through several channels — the post-meeting statement, the press conference, and the Summary of Economic Projections (SEP), whose "dots" show participants' rate paths. Debate over these tools is not new: the committee discussed communications changes last year and could not reach consensus. subject: US Economics Analyst: AI and (Measured) Inflation: Up Then Down
summary: Backdrop. CPI and PCE are built differently even where they share inputs. CPI weights come from the Consumer Expenditure survey, which asks households to exclude business-related purchases; PCE weights come from an Economic Census question asking businesses how much software they sell to individuals — a question that can sweep in software households mainly use for work. Combining PCE's much larger software weight with a price index whose composition was set for CPI is what lets a spike in a small sub-item move the aggregate more than spending shares justify.

subject: US Economics Analyst: The Impact of the World Cup on the US Economy
summary: Method & verdict. [Reasonable] The note blends bottom-up and top-down estimates from genuine historical analogues — the 1994 US World Cup, two decades of Super Bowls, and three US Summer Olympics — scaling 1994 payroll paths up ~30% for the larger 2026 event and building fan spending from per-traveler figures across transport, lodging, food, and tickets. GDP is cross-checked via Gross State Product effects of past Super Bowls, rescaled by relative employment effects and a 1.5 tourism multiplier; inflation combines a category build (hotels, restaurants, transport, adjusted for MSA weights and reservation-timing) with a host-vs-non-host city CPI comparison. The dual approach and use of real comparable events are strengths. Limits are inherent: small samples, wide cross-event variance (especially for inflation), reliance on assumed displacement (one-third) and audience shares, and acknowledged omitted effects like security spending and match-hour productivity loss.

summary: Method & verdict. subject: US Daily: How Will the BLS’s New Birth-Death Methodology Affect the Payrolls Report?
summary: Backdrop. The establishment (payrolls) survey does not capture employment at newly opening firms, and comprehensive data on openings from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) arrives only months after the fact. The BLS therefore estimates the net contribution of business formation in real time with its "birth-death model." It first drops job losses at closing firms, then assumes opening firms grow at the same rate as continuing firms, and finally projects forward the historical error from that procedure — the "birth-death residual" — which captures the tendency for openings to exceed closings and to grow faster than continuing businesses. Until recently, that residual was forecast purely from the time pattern of past residuals.

It assembles three lines of evidence to explain the half-century decline in US construction productivity: (1) industry patent and machine-adoption data showing technological change has been incremental since the 1950s and that innovation spillovers from booming sectors (information, communication, chemicals) barely reach construction's supply chain; (2) a new cross-country land use regulation dataset (Jebwab, Barr and Brueckner, 2021) showing regulations tightened across advanced economies over 50 years, most severely in the US; and (3) measurement analysis, drawing on Garcia and Molloy (2023), documenting a downward bias in US real construction output from unmeasured quality gains and an inappropriate deflator for nonresidential structures.

subject: US Economics Analyst: Productivity Stagnation in the Construction Industry: An International Perspective
summary: The innovation story is one of an industry technologically frozen. The core machines were already in place by the 1950s, adoption of both machinery and pre-fabrication peaked in the 1960s and then receded, and the great productivity booms of recent decades happened in sectors too distant from construction's supply chain to spill over. **The result is that technology lifted construction productivity by only 0.8pp a year, well short of the 1–1.3pp seen elsewhere — a boost that was then entirely offset by other forces.**

subject: Global Markets Daily: All hands on deck to fix US housing affordability?
summary: The case. - **The $200bn GSE MBS purchase program has already lowered mortgage rates, but the gain may not last.** Fannie and Freddie are carrying out the buying, and agency MBS production coupon spreads have tightened ~14-15bp — a move judged consistent with a program of this size and therefore fully priced in. Rates are now near their lowest since September 2022. With a cumulative ~80bp decline since June 2025, a sub-6% rate into the spring season could lift existing home sales by at least 5-7% in 2026 versus 2025, aided by pent-up demand. The catch: MBS spreads are already fair-to-tight, with OAS at QE-era levels, so further tightening needs new policy. If this purchase is a one-off with no follow-through from the GSEs, Fed, or Treasury, spreads likely end the year wider — meaning the recent rate drop could reverse. Pushing new Fed leadership to reinvest portfolio run-off into MBS is one way the support could be extended.

subject: US Daily: December CPI Preview
summary: Unpacked. The headline story in December is mechanical, not fundamental. summary: Backdrop. Labor-market softness this year has come mainly from low hiring rather than rising separations. summary: Backdrop. US official shelter inflation in the CPI and PCE reports is measured from rents across all leases, most of which are continuing leases for existing tenants. subject: US Daily: What Can the Producer Price Index Tell Us About Inflation?
summary: Method & verdict. [Reasonable] The analysis pairs simple correlation tests — same-month core PPI vs. core CPI, and PPI surprises vs. CPI surprises — with a constructed set of intermediate-demand indices. These are built by aggregating thousands of industry- and commodity-level PPI series for each PCE component according to the BEA input-output tables, selecting the best-performing combination of upstream supply-chain stage and lag per component, and netting out estimated indirect tariff effects to avoid double-counting before feeding them into a bottom-up core PCE model. The approach is careful and transparent about its own limits: the sample for services is short (PPI services indices begin only in 2010, alternate core measures only in 2014), and the lag/stage selection is fitted to historical performance, which invites overfitting.

subject: Global Markets Analyst: Predicting Volatility Spikes
summary: Method & verdict. [Reasonable] The study defines volatility as the 60-day exponentially weighted standard deviation of daily yield changes and attacks the breakout question from several angles: Hidden Markov regime-switching to classify vol states, a GARCH model for the pure statistical baseline, a logit model fed by three macro PCA factors (growth, inflation, policy) using level and momentum, and a random forest over a wider economic dataset (employment, inflation, activity, sentiment) to capture non-linearities and interactions. Each model estimates the probability of realized vol breaching thresholds over the next ~125 days, and the same setup compares ex ante implied against ex post realized vol. The multi-model triangulation and out-of-sample tuning of the random forest are strengths; the authors are candid about the limits — none of these can predict pure shocks (they gauge vulnerability, not timing), regime-switch endpoints are hard to anticipate, and random-forest attributions rely on Shapley approximations that are less precise than linear betas.

Unitless measures are converted to GDP terms by regressing changes in the growth measures on 1y and 1y1y consensus forecast revisions, and a priced growth level is inferred from an assumed alignment anchor. summary: Two estimation routes carry most of the weight, and they are deliberately kept as mutual checks. The VAR encodes the economic intuition directly through sign restrictions: a growth shock lifts both equities and yields, while a hawkish policy shock lifts yields but pushes equities down. **Its strength is decomposing each day's move into simultaneous growth and policy contributions; its weakness is that it struggles beyond US growth and US policy**, and the various third-shock extensions to capture non-US, risk-premium, inflation or supply dynamics are acknowledged as less robust. The PCA factor method fills exactly that gap — it reads non-US growth, and therefore FX and non-US equities, more reliably — but at the cost of treating every asset move as demand-driven, so it can misread policy- or supply-led rises in yields as growth improvements.

subject: Global Markets Analyst: The Supply/Demand Drivers of Higher G10 Long-End Risk Premium (Marshall/Freycenet/Zu)
summary: Backdrop. Long-end government yields reflect expected policy rates plus a term premium — compensation for holding duration. That premium is shaped by who owns the debt: central banks and foreign official reserve managers are price-insensitive holders, while pensions, insurers, and asset managers demand compensation that varies with supply, hedging needs, and risk appetite. "Free float" — the share of debt held by the private sector — rises when deficits expand and when central banks run down balance sheets under quantitative tightening.

summary: Backdrop. The Dollar sits at the center of the international monetary system, which makes Dollar assets the default safe asset for official and private investors beyond pure risk-return calculation. subject: Top of Mind: Data (un)reliability
summary: Backdrop. Official statistics — payrolls, inflation, employment levels — are produced by government agencies such as the BLS and used as the reference point for policy, markets, and inflation-linked contracts. subject: India: Strong domestic growth cushions trade drag and pushes up our CY25 growth estimates

summary: Unpacked. The Nakamura, Riblier and Steinsson paper reframes the post-pandemic policy debate. Deviations from the Taylor Rule have been frequent since the 1990s and are not, in themselves, evidence of a policy mistake. **The "long and variable lags" of monetary policy mean a central bank should not fully offset a transitory shock, because rate hikes would hit the economy too slowly to counteract it anyway.** What kept inflation anchored despite the softer response was credibility: banks with strong inflation-fighting records held long-run expectations in place, while those without tightened earlier and more aggressively yet suffered bigger spikes.

subject: US Daily: What Do Customs Data Tell Us About How Much the Effective Tariff Rate Has Risen? (Peng/Phillips)
summary: - **Tariffs take 2–4 months to show up in revenue because of payment and shipping lags.** Importers on the automated system can defer payment for up to 1.5 months, so July revenue partly reflects June imports; comparing July revenue to June imports shows payment delays alone cut the June realized rate by ~0.3pp. On top of that, seaborne shipments take a month or more to arrive and goods already in transit when tariffs were announced are exempt — worth another ~0.4pp. Product-level data confirm the ramp: only 26% of Chinese imports faced the February 10% tariff in month one, rising to 85% and then 96%; EU products went from 20% in April to 80% in May; the auto/parts effective rate took about two months to converge on the estimated 14pp.

subject: Global Markets Analyst: FX Positioning – Follow the Fast Money
summary: Method & verdict. subject: Global Markets Analyst: FX Positioning – Follow the Fast Money
summary: Beta-adjusted risk reversals are the strongest signal. Raw risk reversals embed a structural skew — high-beta pairs carry expensive puts, like equity indices — so the adjustment measures each pair's distance from the beta-vs-risk-reversal line of best fit, isolating cyclical sentiment from hedging demand. **The resulting trading rules diverge more steeply than the volume rules, and short positioning reliably translates into further depreciation.** The effect is a gradual drift rather than event-driven jumps, survives in both higher and lower vol regimes, and outlasts an equivalent carry strategy.

subject: US Daily: Section 899: A Potential Deterrent to Foreign Investment in the US (Phillips/Marshall/Snider/Cahill)
summary: Backdrop. US tax treaties and the 1984 portfolio interest exception currently shield most foreign holders of US debt from withholding, hold treaty dividend and remittance withholding rates low (often ~5%), and leave most foreign capital gains untaxed. The BEAT, enacted in 2017, acts as an alternative minimum tax that adds back deductible payments to foreign affiliates — services, interest, rent, royalties, depreciation — and taxes them at 10%, but only for larger firms with substantial foreign-affiliate dealings. The 2017 BEAT already shifted foreign-bank subsidiary funding toward onshore dollar-raising over the fx swap market, though that trend has since reversed and net amounts due to related foreign offices now sit at all-time highs as fx-implied funding costs compressed.

subject: US Daily: Section 899: A Potential Deterrent to Foreign Investment in the US (Phillips/Marshall/Snider/Cahill)
summary: At issue. H.R. 1, the House-passed fiscal package, would create a new Section 899 of the tax code. It merges two earlier proposals aimed at pressuring countries to rescind taxes affecting US companies — the OECD Pillar Two UTPR, diverted profits taxes, and digital services taxes. Section 899 deems these taxes discriminatory per se (with Treasury discretion to designate others), labeling the imposing countries "discriminatory foreign countries" (DFCs). Individuals, businesses, trusts, funds, and governments resident in DFCs — plus US entities they majority-own — would face the higher taxes described above. The original legislation was sponsored by Rep. Jason Smith and first introduced in 2023, before the current administration.

subject: Global Markets Daily: An External Imbalance Perspective on the EURUSD Cross-Currency Basis (Freycenet/Schaper)
summary: Backdrop. The cross-currency basis is the premium or discount paid to swap funding from one currency into another; a negative EUR basis means paying up to obtain USD. The note frames current pricing against the intermediation environment created after the crises: post-GFC regulation makes arbitraging the basis costly in balance-sheet terms, so funding premiums no longer get competed away as they were pre-crisis. A separate strand of academic work ties bases to global asset exposures and FX-market frictions — external imbalances build up financial claims abroad (the NIIP), those claims generate hedging demand at a ratio sensitive to volatility and risk-reward, and limited intermediation capacity then opens the basis.

subject: Global Markets Daily: An External Imbalance Perspective on the EURUSD Cross-Currency Basis (Freycenet/Schaper)
summary: The more novel move is to widen the lens. **Framing the basis as a function of external imbalances turns it from an ECB story into a global saving-investment story, in which the euro area's growing creditor position against the rest of the world — and against the US in particular — is the structural force pulling the basis higher.** The static NIIP relationship across the G10 and the dynamic behaviour in stress episodes are offered as two independent confirmations that imbalances, not just central-bank balance sheets, price the basis.

subject: US Economics Analyst: SALT Deduction Caps and Interstate Migration (Briggs)
summary: The fiscal channel is where the analysis lands. subject: US Daily: Drug Pricing Policy Changes Will Probably Have Modest Effects on Inflation (Abecasis)
summary: Backdrop. US inflation is tracked by two main gauges that treat healthcare differently. Core PCE weights spending by who ultimately pays, so it captures the large publicly funded share of Medicare and Medicaid; core CPI weights only out-of-pocket and insurance-premium spending by urban consumers, giving government-funded healthcare little to no weight. This asymmetry is why drug-pricing policy — which acts largely on Medicare — registers more in PCE than CPI. Within Medicare, Part B covers drugs administered by professionals, while Part D covers ordinary retail drug spending; the two are captured by different index components, and Medicaid prices are set by statute and largely outside administrative reach.

In real terms, combined with CPI, the estimate is for a 0.4% monthly increase and a 1.1% three-month annualized average.

subject: US Economics Analyst: How Much Will the Effective Tariff Rate Rise? (Peng/Phillips/Mericle)
summary: Backdrop. The US effective tariff rate is the trade-weighted average duty on imports; multiplying tariff changes by prior-year import shares is the standard "naïve" way to estimate its shift. That method breaks down under very large, uneven tariffs because it ignores two behavioral responses seen in the 2018–2019 trade war: imports of heavily taxed goods fall, and sourcing moves toward countries facing lower rates. Import responsiveness is nonlinear — a hike from a low starting rate prompts large substitution, while a hike on an already-high rate does less, because the goods still imported are hard to replace or come from a dominant supplier.

On April 2, 2025, President Trump announced by executive order a two-tier "reciprocal" tariff policy: a universal 10% base tariff (effective April 5) and a country-specific additional tariff (effective April 9), calculated as half the ratio of the US bilateral trade deficit to imports from the country. The order excludes products already subject to, or candidates for, sector-specific tariffs (Sec. 232) and energy, exempts USMCA-compliant goods from Canada and Mexico, limits the levy to non-US content when at least 20% of the content is of US origin, and — in a separate order — revokes de minimis treatment for shipments from China.

summary: Backdrop. Because Republicans hold thin majorities in both chambers, they are advancing tax and spending changes through budget reconciliation, which shields a bill from Senate filibuster and needs only 51 votes rather than 60. summary: Backdrop. US assets have carried heavy overweight positioning for years, a key pillar of the Dollar's elevated valuation over the past decade and of its role as a global safe haven. summary: Method & verdict. [Robust] The framework rests on weekly FX returns from 2010 to present, regressed on interpolated nominal and real yield curves and a defined set of market variables. subject: Global Economics Analyst: Quantifying Global Growth and Inflation Risks from Tariffs (Briggs/Dong/Peters)
summary: Method & verdict. [Reasonable] The analysis runs a pre-existing multi-channel global tariff model — three price channels (direct/indirect pass-through, dollar appreciation, Phillips-curve wage drag) and four GDP channels (real-income hit, investment uncertainty, net-trade reallocation, financial-conditions spillback) solved jointly under a Taylor rule with a dampened price coefficient (0.5 vs 1.5). To move from the baseline to a full risk distribution, it assigns subjective probabilities to eight discrete policy scenarios (e.g. 25% for a cumulative 60pp China tariff, 45% for global autos, 35% for a 10% universal tariff), imposes substitution/inclusion restrictions on joint delivery, layers a three-point retaliation distribution (20% none / 60% partial / 40% full... 20% full), and simulates the joint outcome per economy. The channel structure and explicit percentiles are strengths; the results hinge heavily on hand-set scenario probabilities and modelling assumptions (muted central-bank response, capped uncertainty drag, 33% partial retaliation), and the authors flag exchange-rate moves as the main uncovered source of larger price swings.

subject: US Daily: Less of a Q1 Bump in Inflation (Walker)
summary: The core mechanism is the "January effect," a form of residual seasonality. Firms that reset prices at the start of the year raise them more when inflation is high, but seasonal factors are only calibrated to average January moves — so when the trailing year runs hot, January inflation overshoots. **Because inflation has moderated over the past year, that overshoot has less room to run.** It concentrates in categories with a high share of annual price changes in January — auto fees, food services and accommodations, health care services. Reinforcing the fade, the seasonal adjustment itself has adapted: the real-time hurdle for January core CPI rose from 0.07pp in 2017 to 0.16pp in 2024 and could climb further as this week's CPI seasonal-factor revisions absorb 2024's moves. A third piece of last year's spike was simply noise — a spurious jump in owners' equivalent rent — with no reason to recur.

subject: US Economics Analyst: The End of the Immigration Surge (Peng / Mericle / Phillips)
summary: Backdrop. For most of the pre-pandemic period, US net immigration ran near a trend of about 1mn per year, and the breakeven pace of job growth needed to hold unemployment steady was correspondingly higher. From 2022 to 2024 that trend broke: net immigration surged well above 1mn, peaking at a 3.5–4mn annualized rate in late 2023, overwhelmingly through unauthorized channels — a diverse group spanning asylum seekers, parolees, Temporary Protected Status holders, and people entering illegally. That surge lifted labor-force growth and, arriving when the labor market was the tightest in US history, likely helped cool especially hot low-wage wage growth.

summary: Method & verdict. summary: The three channels distort statistics differently, and keeping them separate is what makes the decomposition work. **Entrepot trade — routing Chinese goods through Vietnam, Mexico, or other EMs for repackaging or token final assembly — moves bilateral flows but not total imports; underreporting lowers both; mislabeling as a lower-tariff product moves neither headline nor bilateral totals, only the product code.** Incentives also differ: entrepot exists only when rates vary across countries, mislabeling only when they vary across goods, while the pull to underreport is always present.

subject: US Economics Analyst: Borrowing From Abroad: Digging into the Decline in the US’s Net International Investment Position (Abecasis)
summary: Backdrop. The NIIP measures US-owned assets abroad minus foreign-owned assets in the US. Its change over time roughly equals the sum of four forces: the trade balance; capital gains or losses from asset-price and exchange-rate swings; a yield differential between US assets held abroad and foreign assets held in the US; and a net-position differential, whereby a larger liability stock grows faster than the asset stock for a given return. The US has long run persistent trade deficits yet avoided a proportionate NIIP decline, thanks to the "exorbitant privilege" — consistently higher returns on its foreign assets than foreigners earn on their US assets, concentrated in FDI. Because it issues the global reserve currency and is the world's largest economy, the US can likely sustain a more negative NIIP than other countries.

summary: Backdrop. The debt ceiling caps total federal borrowing.
